title: Quinoa vs. Lentils: Protein, Fiber, and Carbs Compared

seo.title: Quinoa vs. Lentils: Protein, Fiber, and Carbs Compared
seo.meta_description: Per 100 g cooked, lentils provide about 9 g protein and 8 g fiber; quinoa about 4.4 g protein and 2.8 g fiber. Their carbohydrate totals are similar.
seo.search_intent: Compare cooked quinoa and lentils for protein, fiber, carbohydrates, and calories.

excerpt: Lentils clearly lead on protein and fiber: per 100 g cooked they provide roughly 9 g protein and 8 g fiber, compared with about 4.4 g and 2.8 g in quinoa. Calories and carbohydrate are much closer, so the two foods play different roles on a plate.
content_html:
Quinoa and lentils often appear in the same plant-protein conversation, but they play different roles on a plate. With surprisingly similar calories and carbohydrate per 100 grams cooked, lentils provide about twice the protein and almost three times the fiber. Quinoa behaves more like a grain base and contributes a different texture and amino-acid pattern.

The comparison only works when both foods are measured in the same state. Dry lentils and dry quinoa absorb substantial water during cooking, so 100 grams dry cannot be compared directly with 100 grams cooked if the goal is to picture a serving on your plate.

Cooked nutrition per 100 g

QuinoaLentils
Calories~120~116
Protein~4.4 g~9 g
Carbohydrate~21 g~20 g
Fiber~2.8 g~8 g

Energy differs by only a few calories and carbohydrate by roughly one gram. The gap that changes the meal is protein and fiber: lentils provide about 4.6 grams more protein and more than 5 grams extra fiber per 100 grams cooked.

At a 200-gram serving, that becomes roughly 18 grams of protein and 16 grams of fiber from lentils versus about 9 grams of protein and 5–6 grams of fiber from quinoa. Exact values shift with variety, cooking method, and how much water remains in the finished food.

The rest of the plate matters too. Quinoa paired with tofu, fish, chicken, eggs, or Greek yogurt can be part of a very high-protein meal. Lentils may serve as the central protein-and-fiber component with vegetables and a grain on the side. Food-level numbers do not determine the composition of the entire meal.

Quinoa's advantage is different: protein quality

Quinoa contains all nine essential amino acids and is relatively rich in lysine compared with many cereal grains. That describes the pattern of its protein, not a large total protein amount. A food can have a balanced amino-acid profile and still contribute fewer protein grams per serving than another food.

Lentils also contain all essential amino acids, although legumes are generally relatively lower in methionine than some other foods. You do not need to combine complementary plant proteins in every bite; a varied eating pattern across the day can provide the required amino acids.

Both statements can therefore be true at once: quinoa has an interesting protein profile for a grain-like staple, and lentils still deliver substantially more protein at the same cooked weight. Keeping quality and quantity separate prevents the “complete protein” label from becoming misleading.

Lentils can anchor the protein; quinoa is usually the base

A 180–200 gram serving of lentils can make a substantial contribution to both protein and fiber, allowing the legume to function as the main component of a bowl, soup, or salad. The high fiber amount also contributes bulk and can support fullness, although individual gastrointestinal tolerance varies.

The same weight of quinoa provides less of each nutrient and functions more like rice, couscous, or bulgur: a carbohydrate-rich foundation with some protein, fiber, and minerals. If your goal is a clearly high-protein meal, quinoa usually benefits from a dedicated protein source alongside it.

Tolerance and dietary needs can also decide the choice. Some people build legume portions gradually because large servings cause digestive discomfort. Others value quinoa because it is naturally gluten-free or because its lighter texture fits a particular meal. Nutrient rankings are useful information, not instructions to ignore those differences.

You do not have to choose one or the other

Quinoa and lentils work especially well together. Quinoa contributes separate, grain-like pieces while lentils add protein and fiber. Vegetables, herbs, olive oil, nuts, seeds, or a flavorful dressing can turn that combination into a balanced bowl without asking either ingredient to provide everything.

You can also use them at different meals: quinoa as a side at lunch and lentils as the legume base of dinner. Variety brings different textures and makes the nutrition comparison more useful than treating one food as a permanent replacement for the other.

If the specific question is which provides more protein and fiber by cooked weight, lentils win clearly. If you want a versatile gluten-free grain substitute with a favorable amino-acid pattern, quinoa serves a different purpose. Their similar calories and carbohydrates make the contrast in protein and fiber especially informative.

faq.question: Which has more protein?
faq.answer: Cooked lentils, about 9 g/100 g versus roughly 4.4 g/100 g for quinoa.

faq.question: Which has more fiber?
faq.answer: Lentils, close to 8 g/100 g versus about 2.8 g/100 g for quinoa.

faq.question: Which has more carbohydrate?
faq.answer: They are very similar by cooked weight, around 20–21 g per 100 g.
